title: Kindness, read again
hookLine: the loving-kindness discourse, read whole, start to finish
carry: as a mother her only child
last: WHAT SOMEONE DOES, NOT WHERE THEY'RE FROM.

lines: THE EIGHTH POEM IN THE BOOK.
cards: A radio edit trims a song down. Then one day the full album version plays, with the verse the radio left out, and the same song is suddenly bigger.
More than a year ago, in the first months of this path, there were days on loving-kindness, metta, and its picture of a mother and her child.
Now, reading the Sutta Nipata in order, the poem itself arrives, the eighth piece in the book. Ten short verses, heard start to finish, to notice the shape.

teach.b: The poem moves in three steps. First, how to live.

Before any wishing, it describes a person: capable, upright, gentle, easy to speak to, not proud, content, not weighed down by busyness, calm in the senses, not greedy with families, doing nothing the wise would criticize.
Kindness starts as a way of behaving. Second, the wishes. May all beings be happy and at ease.

Weak or strong, long or short, big or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born: may all beings be happy. Let no one deceive another or look down on anyone anywhere, or wish harm on anyone in anger.
Then the image at the center: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let one cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings.

teach.h: A MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD
teach.b: It's the boundlessness being compared: a love that doesn't measure. Third, the reach.
Kindness spreading above, below and all around, without obstruction, hatred or enmity. Standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as you're awake, keep this mindfulness.
This, the poem says, is called a divine way of living, right here. And the last verse turns.
It ends not on love but on seeing: not grasping at views, having clear vision, letting go of greed for sense pleasures, such a one won't be born again into a womb.

teach.h: AS A MOTHER HER ONLY CHILD.
teach.b: Kindness, in this poem, isn't only warm. It's a path to waking up.

how: The Karaniya Metta Sutta is chanted in Pali in Theravada temples and homes, often from memory, as one of the protective chants called paritta.

games.q: you're reading the kindness poem for the first time. it's about to describe the heart it asks for toward all beings. what picture does it use?
o: a mother protecting her only child with her life.
games.why: a mother and her only child: the comparison is to love without measure, spread to every being.

practice: Say the wishes slowly, in the poem's order: may all beings be happy and at ease, the weak and the strong, the seen and the unseen, the near and the far, those born and those yet to be born.
Then picture the mother bent over her only child, and let that same unmeasured care spread above you, below you, all around. If you know the Pali, you can chant it instead.

wordCard.voice: Kindness. Metta, as the poem lays it out whole: a way of living, a set of wishes for all beings, and a boundless heart spreading in every direction. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali metta (Sanskrit maitri): loving-kindness, friendliness, from mitta, friend.

carryVoice: Your line: as a mother her only child. A heart that doesn't measure. That's day five hundred eighty-five.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (also Khuddakapatha 9)
